Sometimes they used for it the *if'tial* pattern, like *irtada* (he put on a cloak) and *i'tazara* (he wrapped a waist-wrap).

The original form of *al-muzzammil* is *al-mutazammil*; the *ta'* was assimilated into the *za'* after being changed to *za'*, because of their closeness.

Al-Zuhri and the majority of the commentators said that this wrapping to which the verse refers is the wrapping that occurred in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Wrap me up, wrap me up" (*zammiluni zammiluni*), when he came down from the cave of Hira after there had been revealed to him ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1] and the verses that follow it, as in the hadith of Urwa from Aisha in the Book of the Beginning of Revelation in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, although that hadith does not mention the revelation of this surah at that time. Accordingly, it is a literal meaning.

It was also said that it is what is in the hadith of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: "When Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house), they said: 'Give this man a name by which people will turn away from him'—that is, describe him with a description on which people agree. They said: 'A soothsayer,' and they said: 'A madman,' and they said: 'A sorcerer.' The polytheists agreed upon describing him as 'a sorcerer.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he grieved, and he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself. Then Jibril came to him and said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up!﴾ ﴿O you who are covered!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1]."

It will come in surah al-Muddaththir that the reason for its revelation was his seeing the angel seated on a throne between heaven and earth; he returned to Khadija with his heart trembling, and said, "Cover me" (*dath-thiruni*). So it is established that the reason for his being called with ﴿O you who are wrapped up!﴾ was at his saying "Wrap me up," which was when he was distressed by the polytheists' description of him as mad, and that this is different from the reason for his being called with ﴿O you who are covered!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1] in surah al-Muddaththir.

It was also said that it is a wrapping in preparation for the prayer, so he was called ﴿O you who are wrapped up! Stand (in prayer) through the night, except for a little﴾. This is related from Qatada, and close to it from al-Dahhak. These opinions are close to each other.

Its interpretation according to the literal meaning of the wrapping is clear. Ikrima said: its meaning is "I have wrapped this matter (on you), so stand up to it," meaning the matter of prophethood. Then his saying ﴿through the night, except for a little﴾ together with his saying ﴿Indeed, for you in the day is extended occupation﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 7] is an exhortation to exert one's full effort in carrying out the task of conveying the message at all times, by night and by day, except for a little of the night, which is what one is compelled to sleep. In his view, the wrapping is to be understood metaphorically.

If surah al-Muzzammil was revealed before surah al-Muddaththir, that indicates that God, after He had begun His Messenger with revelation through the opening of the surah ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾, then revealed to him the surah al-Qalam to refute the polytheists' statement about him, which al-Walid ibn al-Mughira had arranged, that they should say: "He is mad."

He revealed to him gentleness in addressing him as he wrapped himself in his garments because of the grief that had come upon him from the polytheists' words. So God commanded him to ward off that by standing in prayer at night. Then the revelation paused. When he saw the angel who had been sent to him at Hira, he covered himself because of the intensity of the impact of that vision, and so He revealed to him ﴿O you who are covered!﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1].

Thus the Prophet's (ﷺ) being called with the description of *al-muzzammil* is in regard to his state at the time of the call. *Al-Muzzammil* is not counted among the names of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Suhayli said: "He was not known by it." Some people went so far as to count it among his names.

The verb *qum* (stand) is used intransitively, so it does not need an object to be supplied, because standing here means prayer. This standing is different from the standing commanded in surah al-Muddaththir by His saying ﴿Stand and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 2], for that means beginning (the mission), as will come there.

*Al-layl* (the night) is the time of darkness from after the 'isha' prayer until dawn. *Al-layl* is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*), so the command requires prayer throughout the whole time of the night. It is known that times for relieving oneself from needs, such as dozing in sleep and the like, are excepted from the requirements of human necessities.

*Qiyam al-layl* (night prayer) is a term in the terminology of the Qur'an and the Sunna for the prayer performed at night, excluding the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers and their regular supererogatory prayers.

The command to the Messenger to perform night prayer is a command of obligation and is specific to him, because the address is directed to him alone, like the surahs that preceded the revelation of this surah. As for night prayer for the Muslims, they followed the Messenger (ﷺ) in it, as will come in His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer)﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], up to His saying ﴿and a group of those with you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and the verses. The majority said that this was before the five daily prayers were prescribed for the times of the day and night.

Perhaps the wisdom of this standing that was made obligatory upon the Messenger (ﷺ) at the beginning of his mission is that his inner being would grow in purity through it, strengthening his readiness to receive revelation, so that revelation would not overwhelm him as it pressed upon him when it first descended, as is related in the hadith of al-Bukhari: "It squeezed me until I reached the limit of my strength, then he said: Read in the name of your Lord" (the hadith). This wisdom is supported by His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5].

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to seclude himself (*yatahannathu*) in the cave of Hira shortly before his prophethood, by inspiration from God the Exalted. So He who inspired him with that before revelation came to him is fitting to command him to it after revelation came to him, so that there would not remain any period of time in which he was not devoted to worship. For this reason we prefer the view that night prayer was made obligatory upon him before the five daily prayers were made obligatory upon him and upon the community.

The obligation of night prayer continued upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) after the five daily prayers were made obligatory, as an honour to his station, through his abundant turning to intimate conversation with his Lord in the time of his leisure from conveying revelation and managing the affairs of the Muslims. That time is the night, as His saying indicates: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud (voluntary night prayer) with it as an extra (prayer) for you; perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79], meaning an increase in closeness for you. It was previously discussed in surah al-Isra'. So this was a ruling specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the jurists mentioned it in the section on the particularities of the Prophet (ﷺ). It was not obligatory upon others, and no prayer was prescribed for the Muslims before the five daily prayers. Rather, the Muslims used to follow the Prophet's (ﷺ) practice, and he approved them in that, so they regarded it as binding upon themselves. God praised them for that in many verses, such as His saying ﴿Their sides forsake their beds﴾ [al-Sajda: 16]. This will come at His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) nearly two-thirds of the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and the verse.

Aisha said: "God made night prayer obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Prophet and his companions stood (in prayer)," although there is no dispute that the obligation of standing (in night prayer) was lifted from the Muslims. It is established that it is recommended for them. There is disagreement about whether its obligation continued for the Prophet (ﷺ), and there is no benefit in pursuing evidence for or against that.

His saying *illa qaliluan* (except for a little) is an exception from *al-layl* (the night), meaning: except for a little of it. So the obligation of standing did not attach to him for all the hours of the night.

*Nisfahu* (half of it) is an exact substitute (*badal mutabiq*) for *qalilan* (a little), and it is an explanation of the vagueness of *qalilan*. So here He made the "little" to be half or a little less than half.

The benefit of this vagueness is to hint that it is better for the standing to be more than half the night, and that making it half the night is a mercy and a concession for the Prophet (ﷺ). This is supported by its being followed by His saying ﴿or subtract from it a little﴾, meaning: subtract a little from the half, so that the time of standing in the night is less than half of it, and that is then "little." So it is a concession within a concession.

He said ﴿or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4], which returns to encouragement that the duration of standing be more than half the night. For this reason He did not restrict "or add to it" with the same restriction as "or subtract from it," so that the addition beyond half would be unlimited. It is recorded in the hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) took the stricter course and stood (in prayer) until his feet swelled. It was said to him about that: "God has forgiven you what came before of your sin and what came after," and he said: "Should I not be a grateful servant?"

The choice indicated by the particle *aw* (or) is considered in relation to the variation of nights in length and shortness, because that is connected to the breadth of the day for work and for taking one's missed share of sleep.

Furthermore, that is an extension for the Prophet (ﷺ) to remove the hardship of a fixed time for standing, so the matter was approached by way of facilitation.

Ibn Atiyya made *al-layl* a generic noun that applies to all nights, and the meaning: "except for a little of the nights," which are the nights in which there is an excuse that prevents him from standing in them. That is, it is an exception from the nights in terms of their individual instances, not in terms of their parts. Then He said *nisfahu* (half of it), and so on to the end.

The restriction of the night to prayer is because it is customarily the time of sleep, so commanding the Messenger (ﷺ) to stand in it is an increase in occupying his times with turning to intimate conversation with God. Also because the night is a time of quiet of voices and of people's occupations, so the soul of the one who stands in it is better prepared to receive the divine outpouring.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 4:

﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured tones (tartil)﴾. It may be connected to the night prayer, meaning: recite your recitation during the standing (qiyam) in prayer.

It may also be an independent command about the manner of reciting the Qur'an, which was mentioned in connection with the command to stand in prayer at night. This second reading is preferable, because recitation in prayer falls within it. The revelation of this surah was at the beginning of the period of the Qur'an's descent, so the whole of the Qur'an at the time this surah was revealed was two or three surahs, based on the most accurate opinions that this amount of the surah is Meccan, and that this surah is among the early surahs. This is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5], i.e., We will reveal to you a Qur'an.

So the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to recite the Qur'an slowly and clearly.

Tartil (measured, distinct articulation) means making a thing arranged (murattal), i.e., separated. Its origin is from their saying: thaghr murattal, which is a mouth with teeth that are spaced apart, i.e., with the teeth slightly separated so that the molars do not press against each other. Tartil of the Qur'an is meant as tartil of its recitation, i.e., moving slowly in pronouncing the letters of the Qur'an until they come out of the mouth clearly, with the vowels that deserve it being prolonged. 'A'isha described tartil, saying: "If a listener wished to count its letters, he could count them, not like your recitation this (hasty) way."

The benefit of this is that its memorization becomes firm, and listeners receive it so that it clings to their memories, and that its reader and listener reflect on its meanings, so that the tongue's utterance does not precede the work of understanding. Someone said to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "I recited the Mufassal (the later, shorter surahs) in one night." 'Abd Allah said: "This is like the hasty reciting of poetry, because when they recited a qasida they hurried so that the metre of its meter would appear and its rhymes would follow one another upon the ears." Hadh (hasty reciting) is rapid cutting off (of words).

This command was emphasized with the absolute object (mafʿul muṭlaq) to indicate the realization of the quality of tartil. The majority of reciters (al-Jumhur) read ﴿awi-nqus﴾ with a damma on the waw, to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters when the hamzat al-wasl drops, so they vocalized the waw with a damma to match the damma on the qaf of ﴿unqus﴾ after it. Hamza and 'Asim read it with a kasra on the waw, according to the original rule for escaping the meeting of two unvocalized letters.

Page 261

In His words ﴿or add to it, and recite the Qur'an in measured tones﴾, there occurs, when the fatha on the nun of al-Qur'an is extended, an embellishment of the metre: it becomes one hemistich of the Kamil meter, with the first foot (ahadh) having had idmar (a shortened foot) applied to it twice.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to stand in prayer at night. It came as an interpolation (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical clause inserted between two statements) between the clause (*qumi al-layl*, "stand [in prayer] at night") and the clause ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is more potent in effect (wat'an) and more upright in speech﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 6). It is a resumptive clause (istinaf) of the explanatory kind (istinaf bayani), answering the question of the wisdom behind the command to stand at night. The wisdom is the preparation of the soul of the Prophet (ﷺ) to bear the intensity of revelation. This implies that God made that easy for him, as He said: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ (al-Qiyamah: 17). This is the reason this clause follows ﴿Stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 2). This indicates that the revelation of this verse occurred at the beginning of the Prophet's (ﷺ) period of receiving the Qur'an. When He said to him ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 4), He followed it with the explanation of the reason for the command to recite the Qur'an in measured fashion.

The "weighty word" is the Qur'an, and its being "sent down upon him" (*ilqa'uhu 'alayhi*) means conveying it to him by way of revelation through the angel.

The literal sense of *al-ilqa'* (casting) is throwing an object from the hand to the ground and dropping it. One says *shay' laqan*, meaning "something cast down." The word *ilqa'* was used figuratively for conveying (*ibla'*) suddenly and without anticipation.

The heaviness attributed to the word is undoubtedly a figurative heaviness (*thiql majazi*), used metaphorically for the difficulty of memorizing it, because it contains meanings that are not among the common things that pass through the minds of his people. Thus, memorizing that word would be arduous for the unlettered Messenger, such that his capacity would strain to receive it.

His saying ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ indicates that its heaviness is initially connected to the Messenger (ﷺ), given His previous saying ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you﴾. It is a figurative heaviness in all its aspects: it is heavy and difficult to receive from the One who sent it down upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: When revelation descended upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), it weighed heavily upon him, and his skin would break out (*tarabbada*), that is, change with something like goosebumps. 'A'ishah said: "I saw revelation descend upon him on an extremely cold day, and it would part from him, and his forehead would be dripping with sweat."

The heaviness of the word is also used metaphorically because it contains abundant meanings, the knowledge of which requires fine reflection. This is due to the perfection of its guidance and the abundance of its meanings. Al-Farra' said: "*Thaqilan* means it is not ordinary speech (*al-kalam al-safsaf*)." It is sufficient for you that it contains knowledge and sciences that the intellect cannot fully encompass. How many the understandings of scholars have plunged into it, among jurists, theologians, eloquent speakers, philologists, and philosophers. Thus it resembles a heavy thing in that a single person cannot alone bear its meanings.

The emphasis of this statement with a particle of emphasis (*harf al-ta'kid*) serves to draw attention to it and to inform the Messenger (ﷺ) of the emphasis on its nearness and continuity, so that its arrival would be easier for him than the arrival of a sudden command.

[Page 262]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is more potent in trampling [the soul] and more upright in speech.﴾ This is a justification for singling out the time of the night for standing in prayer therein. It is therefore connected to the sentence (﴿Stand [in prayer] during the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2]), meaning: Stand in prayer during the night, because its rising [of prayer] is more potent in trampling and more upright in speech.

The meaning: in standing in prayer during the night there is purification and clarification of your inner self, and an elevation of you to the angelic levels.

And (nashi'ata) is an adjective derived from al-nashʼ (al-nashʼ), which is coming into being. This adjective has been used here without a noun it qualifies, and it is attached to "the night" with the sense of "in" as in (makr al-layl, the scheming of the night). It has been made among the most upright of speech, so it is known that in it there is speech. The command to stand in the night and to recite the Qur'an had preceded it, so it is determined that its omitted qualified noun is ṣalāh (prayer), meaning: the prayer that arises in the night, for prayer comprises actions and words, and it is standing.

The prayer is described as nāshi'a because the one who prays initiates it, and so it arises after the stillness of the night, and it resembles the cloud that forms on the horizon after a clear sky. When the prayer is after sleep, the sense of arising in it is stronger, and for this reason ʻĀʼishah explained it as standing [in prayer] after sleep. Ibn ʻAbbās explained ﴿nāshi'at al-layl﴾ as the night prayer in its entirety, and Mālik chose this. From ʻAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn it is reported that it is what lies between Maghrib and ʻIshā'. From Ibn Mas'ūd, Ibn ʻAbbās and Saʻīd ibn Jubayr it is reported that the origin of this word is arabicised from Abyssinian (Ḥabashī), and al-Subkī counted it in his poem among the Arabicised words of the Qur'an.

The choice of the word (nāshi'a) in this verse, rather than others such as qiyām (standing) or tahajjud (night vigil), is due to what it may bear of these meanings, so that people may exert effort in understanding it.

The reciters of the ten, the majority (Jumhur al-ʻAshara), read (waṭ'an) with a fatḥah on the wāw and sukūn on the ṭāʼ followed by a hamzah. Al-waṭ' originally means placing the foot on the ground, and here it is used metaphorically for a meaning that suits being a feature of the darkness of the night. It is possible that waṭ' is used metaphorically for an act of the one praying, in the manner of attributing a verbal noun to its doer, meaning: you are the one trampling, so it is metaphorical for the praying person's ability to pray at night, with his freedom for it and the calm of his mind from daytime occupations, like the firmness of one treading on the ground; thus it is more conducive to the act. The meaning: more impactful in effect. Jābir ibn Zayd and al-Ḍaḥḥāk explained it this way, and al-Farrāʼ said it.

It is also possible that waṭ' is metaphorical for the state of night prayer and its effect on the one praying, meaning: the greatest effect of good on his self and the most firmly rooted in goodness and reward. Qatādah explained it this way.

Ibn ʻĀmir and Abū ʻAmr alone read (wiṭā'an) with a kasrah on the wāw, a fatḥah on the ṭāʼ and a madd, the verbal noun of (wāṭa'a), from the root of the pattern (fi'āl). Al-wiṭā' means agreement and harmony, as God the Exalted said: ﴿so that they may agree on the number of what God has forbidden﴾ [al-Tawbah: 37]. The meaning: night prayer is more conducive to the one praying in harmonising the tongue and the heart, meaning between uttering the words and understanding their meanings, because of the stillness that occurs at night and the cessation of distractions. Mujāhid explained it according to this sense.

The pronoun (hiya) is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and see what will come at the words of God the Exalted ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves, you will find it with God, better and greater in reward﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], regarding the occurrence of the pronoun of separation between a definite noun and a comparative adjective. The pronoun of separation here serves to strengthen the judgement, not to restrict it.

Al-aqwam: the better in straightness, which is the absence of crookedness and deviation, and (aqwam) is used metaphorically for the better and more beneficial.

Qīlan: speech, and what is meant by it is the recitation of the Qur'an, given the preceding words ﴿Indeed, We shall send down upon you a heavy word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. The meaning: night prayer is more helpful in recalling the Qur'an and in being safe from forgetting some of its verses, and more helpful for further reflection (tadabbur). Ibn ʻAbbās said: "Aqwamu qīlan: nearer to understanding the Qur'an." Qatādah said: "More retentive for recitation." Ibn Zayd said: "More upright in recitation, because of its freedom from worldly concerns."

(Waṭ'an) and (qīlan) are accusative as specifications (tamyīz) of the comparatives (ashadd) and (aqwam).

Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, for you by day is extended occupation.﴾ The fact that this sentence is set apart without a conjunction (ʿatf) to the preceding one indicates that its content is not of the same kind as the ruling before it. Therefore the intent is not to specify the midday prayer, since according to the well-known view the five daily prayers had not yet been prescribed at that time. At that point, only the night prayer (qiyam al-layl) had been prescribed.

[Page 264]

What appears is that this sentence serves as the reason (ʿillah) for something within the statement ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is more potent in tread and more upright in speech﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 6). This may be understood in two ways. It may be an explanation for choosing the night for the obligation of standing in prayer, so it emphasizes the importance of maintaining the night prayer, because the day cannot substitute for it. The meaning would then be: stand in prayer at night, because its standing has greater impact and its words are more firmly established, since the day is a time filled with great occupation that leaves you no solitude with yourself. The Prophet ﷺ was occupied during the day with calling to God, conveying the Qur'an, teaching the religion, disputing with the polytheists, and checking on the weak believers. All of this is expressed by the phrase "extended occupation." The sentence may also be a gentle excuse for the burden of the night prayer. It contains guidance that the day is a wide space in which to carry out whatever the night prayer might burden one with in terms of lethargy during the day, so that one may sleep part of the day and attend to one's tasks during it.

It is also possible that this sentence is an explanation of what is implied in ﴿or reduce it a little﴾ (al-Muzzammil: 3). That is, if you reduce something from half the night, the reward of its knowledge will not be lost to you, for you have during the day ample room for standing in prayer and recitation, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day in succession for whoever wishes to remember or wishes gratitude﴾ (al-Furqan: 62).

It is established that the Prophet ﷺ prayed during the day from the beginning of his mission, before the five prayers were prescribed, as indicated by His statement: ﴿Have you seen the one who forbids﴾ (al-ʿAlaq: 9), ﴿a servant when he prays?﴾ (al-ʿAlaq: 10). It has already been mentioned in surah al-Jinn that their hearing of the Qur'an occurred during the Prophet's ﷺ prayer with his companions at Nakhlah on their way to ʿUkaz. It appears that all of this is intended, since it is among what the meaning of the phrase ﴿extended occupation﴾ allows, and it is an instance of concise eloquence (ījaz).

The word sabh (سَبْح) originally means swimming, that is, moving the body through abundant water. It is used here as a metaphor (istiʿarah) for easy, wide-ranging activity, resembling the movement of a swimmer in water, for nothing blocks his gliding over the surface of the water, nor does the fatigue of travel on land stop him.

Close to this metaphor is the use of sabh for the running of a horse without strain, in the description by Imru' al-Qays of the horses as "the swimming ones" in his praise of his mount:

*A swift one, which, when the swimming (horses) were worn out, raised dust on the packed ground.*

Here he expresses the running ones as "the swimming ones."

[Page 265]

Ibn ʿAbbas interpreted sabh as free time (al-faragh), that is, to sleep during the day. Ibn Wahb said, on the authority of Ibn Zayd, who said: "A long free time for your needs, so empty yourself for your religion at night."

The word ṭawīl (طويل) is an adjective derived from ṭūl (length), which is the increase in the extension of a person's stature, a road, or a garment beyond the measure of most of its kind. Length is a quality of physical things, but its attribution to time became common, as one says "a long night." In a hadith: "Winter is the spring of the believer: its day is short, so he fasts it, and its night is long, so he stands in prayer through it."

As for describing sabh with ṭawīl in this verse, it is a rational metaphor (majaz ʿaqlī), because what is actually long is the place of swimming, that is, the water in which one swims. Moreover, in His statement ṭawīlan (طَوِيلًا) there is a nurturing or supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor of sabh as work during the day.

﴿Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him, so take Him as your Trustee﴾. This is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to "Stand [in prayer] through the night" (qum al-layl). The unrestricted command, without specifying a time, is intended to convey its generality: that is, remember the name of your Lord at night and in the day, like His saying: ﴿And remember the name of your Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Insan: 25].

The word "name" (ism) is inserted because what is commanded is mention by the tongue, which also encompasses remembrance by the mind, since utterances follow what is in the soul. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and fearfully, and without loud speech﴾ [al-A'raf: 205].

Tabattul (devoted separation) is intensive severance (shiddat al-batl). It is the verbal noun of tabattala, the intransitive form (muṭāwiʿ) of battalahu, and here it bears the figurative sense of muṭāwaʿa, whose form implies an emphasis on the act's occurrence, as though another had done it to him and he complied. Tabattul means separation, and here it is figurative separation: the freeing of one's mind and thought for what pleases God, as if one has withdrawn from people and taken refuge at God's side. Hence it is construed with ila ("to"), which indicates arrival at an endpoint. Imru' al-Qays said:

"A beacon for the evening place of a monk who has devoted himself."

Tabtil is the verbal noun of battala (intensive form), which is a transitive verb, like taqtiʿ (cutting up).

[p. 266]

This verbal noun is used in place of tabattul to indicate that achieving tabattul, that is, separation, requires tabtil, that is, severing. Since tabtil is performed by the one who devotes himself, his tabtil is the cutting of himself off from anyone other than the one to whom he devotes himself. *Al-hajr al-jamil* (the beautiful abandonment) is that which is good in its kind. States and meanings are, among them, good and, among them, bad in their kind. It may be said: noble and blameworthy, pure and turbid. A description applies to a kind by what naturally accompanies it of accidental features that suit the reality of that kind. When the reality is stripped of the accidents that may attach to it, its kind is pure. When something that is not among its properties is attached to the reality, the kind becomes turbid and ugly. This is indicated by His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. It was mentioned earlier at His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ [al-Naml: 29], in Surat al-Naml. In this same sense is His saying (﴿so patience is beautiful﴾ [Yusuf: 18]) in Surat Yusuf, and His saying ﴿so be patient with beautiful patience﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 5] in Surat al-Ma'arij.

Thus the beautiful abandonment is that in which the one who practices it confines himself to the reality of abandonment, which is ceasing to associate with someone, and does not combine it with other harshness or injury. Since abandonment arises from hatred of the one abandoned, or from aversion to his deeds, it is liable to involve harm such as abuse, striking, or the like. So God commanded His Messenger to abandon the polytheists with a beautiful abandonment, that is, to abandon them without going beyond their abandonment with abuse or retaliation.

This abandonment is the Prophet's (ﷺ) restraint from repaying them with the like of what they say, which is what His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and be patient over what they say﴾ indicates.

It does not extend to the call to the religion, for that is continuous; rather it is a conveying from God, may He be exalted, and so it is not attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) drew from this verse an ethical lesson: that God gathered, in these two words, what a person needs in associating with people. For a person either associates with them, and then he must be patient with their harm and their alienation of him, since if he sets his soul on comfort with them he will not find it lasting, and so he falls into distress unless he reconciles his soul to patience with their harm. Or he abandons association, and that is the beautiful abandonment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 11:

﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of plenty, and give them a little respite.﴾ The discussion of it is like the discussion of ﴿So leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ [al-Qalam: 44] in Surat al-Qalam, meaning: leave Me to deal with them. That is, do not concern yourself with their denial, do not occupy yourself with repeatedly responding to them, do not become angry, and do not curse them, for I will suffice you against them.

The word al-mukadhdhibin (the deniers) is in the accusative as an object with (ma'a) (the ma'iyya construction), and the waw is the waw of accompaniment.

The deniers are those whom the pronoun in (they say) and (and forsake them) refers to, namely the deniers of the Prophet ﷺ among the people of Makkah. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is to convey that denial is the cause of this threat.

He described them as ﴿the people of plenty﴾ as a rebuke to them, that they denied because of their delusion and arrogance over the abundance of their circumstances, and as a threat to them that He who said ﴿leave Me with the deniers﴾ will remove that luxury from them.

In this description there is an allusion of mockery, because they used to regard the breadth of life and abundance of wealth as perfection, and they used to reproach those who believed for their poverty. God, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29] ﴿and when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 30], and so on in the verses, and He, exalted is He, said ﴿Those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat﴾ [Muhammad: 12].

The word (ni'mah) here is with a fatha on the nun, by the agreement of the readers. It is a noun for affluence, and its plural is (an'um), with a fatha on the hamza and a damma on the ayn.

As for (ni'mah), with a kasra on the nun, it is a noun for a state agreeable to a person's desire, such as health, security, provision, and the like of what is pleasant. Its plural is (ni'am), with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ayn, and it may be made a sound plural as (ni'amat), with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the ayn, according to the majority of the Arabs. In the dialect of the people of the Hijaz the ayn is pronounced with a kasra in imitation (kasrat ittiba').

As for (nu'mah), with a damma on the nun, it is a noun for joy (al-masarrah), so it may be pluralized as (nu'm), taken as a collective noun, and it may be pluralized as (nu'am), with a damma then a fatha, like (ghurfah) and (ghuraf), and this pattern is regular.

Their being described as ﴿those of plenty﴾ with the nun fathah is to indicate that the utmost of their share in this life is plenty, that is, free movement in living without constraint, enjoying shade of houses and gardens, indulging in sweet foods and the pleasures of enjoyment with women, wine, and gambling, while they turn away from the perfections of the soul and the delight of guidance and knowledge. God, exalted is He, said ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like cattle; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. The definiteness of (al-ni'mah) is for the specific (ahd, a known referent).

Al-tamhil is a strong granting of respite, and al-imhal is postponement and delay of punishment. It is semantically consequent upon His saying ﴿and leave Me with the deniers﴾, meaning: wait for Us to grant you victory, as in His saying ﴿and do not seek to hasten for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35].

And (qalilan) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a little respite. It is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq).

[p. 271]

This is a reason (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. That is: because with Us is what is more severe for them than your rejection of them. This reason conveys a threat: these punishments have been prepared for them because, since they come from the treasuries of God's vengeance, God places them in the places that deserve them, namely those who exchanged God's blessing for disbelief. So God has prepared for them, in the eternal life, the opposite of the foundations of the blessing that was bestowed on them. They grew arrogant with it and met the Benefactor with ingratitude.

Thus the shackles (al-ankal) correspond to their ingratitude for the blessing of health and ability, since al-ankal means fetters. The blazing fire (al-jahim), which is the fire of Hell, corresponds to the pleasure of shade and coolness they had enjoyed. The food that chokes (ta'am dhu ghussah) corresponds to the wholesome foods they had been immersed in: fruits, cooked dishes, and game. Al-ankal is the plural of nakl, pronounced with a fatha or a kasra on the nun and with a sukun on the kaf, and it means a heavy fetter.

Al-ghussah, with a damma on the ghayn, is the name for the effect of choking in the throat. It is the lodging of food and drink in the throat such that the throat cannot swallow it, due to illness, grief, or a sob.

The annexation of "food" to "choking" (idafah) is figurative (majaz), and it is of the type of annexation by the slightest connection (min al-idafah li-adna mulabasah), since choking is an accident in the throat whose cause is food or drink that cannot be swallowed because of its foulness or dryness.

The painful punishment (al-'adhab al-alim) corresponds to the pleasures of human delights that were in the blessing, since pain is the opposite of pleasure. The wise have defined pleasure as the deliverance from pain.

The last item has been put in the plural, as the opposite of the meaning of blessing (with a fatha on the first letter).

The indefiniteness of these four kinds is intended to magnify and terrify. The word "with" (ladá) may be taken in its literal sense, and a noun may be understood between it and the nun of majesty, the sense being "with Our treasuries", that is, the treasuries of punishment. It may also be a figurative expression for the power to bring these things into being whenever God wills.

The phrase ﴿on the day the earth and the mountains quake﴾ is connected to the stable predicate contained in the predicate of "indeed" (inna) in the phrase ﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾.

Al-rajf is shaking and convulsion, and what is meant is a repeated and continuous quaking, by which the parts of the earth are scattered and dissolved.

Al-kathib is sand gathered into a heap like a mound, meaning the stones of the mountains become fine dust.

Mahil is a passive participle from hala al-shay' hayl, when one scatters and pours it out. Its original form is mahyul, the damma being felt heavy on the ya', so it was moved to the preceding unvocalized letter; two unvocalized letters then met, so the waw was deleted, and also because it is an added letter, which the damma indicates.

The verb "were" (kanat) in the phrase ﴿and the mountains were a heap of sand﴾ is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as if it had already happened in the past. The reason it differs in style from "quake" is that the mountains becoming heaps of sand is a strange matter, unusual, and so the listeners may find it hard to believe. As for the quaking of the earth, it is well known, except that this promised quaking is the greatest of what is known of its kind.

The painful punishment (al-'adhab al-alim) corresponds to the pleasures of human delights that were in the blessing, since pain is the opposite of pleasure. The wise have defined pleasure as the deliverance from pain.

The last item has been put in the plural, as the opposite of the meaning of blessing (with a fatha on the first letter).

The indefiniteness of these four kinds is intended to magnify and terrify. The word "with" (ladá) may be taken in its literal sense, and a noun may be understood between it and the nun of majesty, the sense being "with Our treasuries", that is, the treasuries of punishment. Mahil is a passive participle from hala al-shay' hayl, when one scatters and pours it out. As for the quaking of the earth, it is well known, except that this promised quaking is the greatest of what is known of its kind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verses 15–16:

﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger, a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger.﴾ ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a severe seizing.﴾ The speech was shifted to addressing the polytheists after the address had been directed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The occasion for this is the transition to warning them, after He had commanded him to be patient with what they say and to part from them graciously, when He said to him: ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], up to His saying: (﴿and a painful punishment﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 13]).

So the speech is a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and this address is not counted as iltifat (shift of address), because the speech has been shifted to a purpose other than the one that preceded it.

The address here follows the requirement of the apparent sense (muqtada al-zahir) according to both schools: the school of the majority (al-Jumhur) and the school of al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki, the rhetorician).

The purpose of this statement is an allusive (ta'ridh) threat, that there should befall them the like of what befell their predecessors among those who denied the messengers. It is thus an example (mathal) set forth for the polytheists.

This is the first example God set forth for the polytheists to threaten them with the fate of their like, according to the view of the majority concerning the revelation of this surah.

As God related of them in His saying: ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like us, while their people are servants to us?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47]. The people of Makkah also said: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two towns?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]. God has also related of them that they said: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord? The example of Pharaoh has been repeated in the Qur'an as applied to Abu Jahl, who was the leader of those hostile to the Prophet (ﷺ), the instigators against him, and the most stubborn of the chieftains of Quraysh in disbelief.

The report is emphasized with (inna), because the addressees deny that God sent a messenger to them.

He made "messenger" indefinite (nakkara rasulan), because they know the one meant in this speech, and because the locus of the threat and the comparison is not the person of the Messenger (ﷺ) but the attribute of being sent.

Into the comparison and the threat is incorporated the description of the Messenger (ﷺ) as a witness over them.

The meaning of "witness" here is the witnessing of conveying what God wanted of people, and by this the descriptor (shahidan) agrees with the use of the active participle in the present tense: he is a witness over you now, by renewing the call and conveyance.

As for the witnessing of the Messenger (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection, it is a witnessing to the truthfulness of the Muslims in their testimony upon the nations that their messengers conveyed to them the messages of their Lord. "Messenger" is indefinite (tankir rasulan) in reference to the one sent to Pharaoh, because what is considered is the sending, not the person sent, since the comparison relates to the sending in His saying: ﴿as We sent to Pharaoh﴾, its implied sense being "like Our sending to Pharaoh a messenger."

The consequence expressed by ﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger﴾ is an indication that this is the purpose of this report, namely the threat that there befall the addressees, since they disobeyed the Messenger (ﷺ), the like of what befell Pharaoh.

For when an indefinite noun is repeated as definite with the article, its referent is the same as the first.

The verb "seizing" (akhdh) is used metaphorically for destruction, because when He removed them from life, His act resembled the act of one who takes something from its place and places it with himself.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, this is a reminder, so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way.﴾ It is a concluding statement (tadhyil), meaning: it is a reminder for whoever is willing to be reminded. If he is one of those who deny the resurrection, he believes in it; and if he is a believer, he awakens from some of the heedlessness that afflicts the believer, and makes up for what he has missed. By this comprehensive generality, which includes the circumstances of those spoken of and the circumstances of others, the sentence became a concluding statement.

The demonstrative "this" (hadhihi) refers to the verses preceding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you a messenger as a witness against you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 15].

The statement is emphasized with a particle of emphasis (inna), because those initially addressed by it were deniers that the Qur'an is a reminder and guidance. They denied that it was from Allah, and branded it as sorcery and fables. That was among their statements to which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was guided to be patient, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And be patient over what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10].

The word tadhkira (reminder) is the name of the verbal noun of dhikr (with a dammah on the dhal), which is the arising of a thing in the mind. Thus tadhkira means admonition, because it reminds the heedless of the evil consequences. This is an acknowledgment of the verses of the Qur'an and a renewal of the exhortation to reflect upon it and to contemplate it, in the manner of indirect allusion (ta'ridh).

Following upon this indirect exhortation is an explicit exhortation in His saying: ﴿so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾, meaning: whoever wishes to take to his Lord a way, then the taking of a path to Allah has been made ready for him through this reminder, so the heedless has no excuse left.

The use of the relative construction "whoever wills" (man sha'a) is by way of exhortation, because it implies that this path leads to good, so nothing stands between the seeker of good and following this path except his own will, since His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ is an indicator of that. Of this kind is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And say: The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. That is not a permission for belief and disbelief; rather it is an exhortation to belief, and what follows it is a warning against disbelief, meaning: the consequence of negligence in that falls upon the negligent one. For this reason Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is not the permission of the matter and its opposite, but rather it includes the meaning of promise and threat.

In the Tafsir of Ibn 'Arafa, which some of our shaykhs used to interpret as meaning that one is given the choice in determining the path, so the object of the choice in his view is that he should specify some path among the paths, he said: "It is good," so the apparent meaning of the verse remains as it is, with the choice. End quote.

You have known from what we have established that there is no need for this, and that there is nothing in the verse that carries the meaning of choice.

In His saying "to his Lord" there is a simile of the condition of one seeking success and guidance to the condition of one traveling toward a helper or a generous one, who has been shown the path that brings him to his goal, so nothing remains to hinder him from following it.

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand in prayer for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and so do a group of those with you. And Allah determines the night and the day. He knows that you cannot keep count of it, so He has turned to you in mercy. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an.﴾

From here begins what was revealed of this surah at Medina, as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah.

The plain sense of this verse indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to stand in prayer during the night before this verse was revealed, and that a group of his companions used to stand in prayer as well, acting upon the command at the beginning of the surah in His words ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except for a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2], and so on. It is therefore established that this verse was revealed to lighten the burden on all of them, as shown by His words in it, ﴿so He has turned to you in mercy﴾. Thus it is abrogating (nasikh, that which abrogates) the command at the beginning of the surah.

[Page 279]

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed about the time and place of its revelation, and about the relationship between what it requires and what the preceding verse requires. The well-known and reliable view is that the opening of the surah was revealed in Mecca.

One should not be misled by what al-Tabari transmitted from Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'A'isha, which gives the impression that the opening of the surah was revealed in Medina. Similar is what was narrated from al-Nakha'i concerning the wrapping in a cloak (al-tazammul bi-mirt) belonging to 'A'isha.

It is not necessary to dwell at length on the question of whether the standing in prayer prescribed at the beginning of the surah was an obligation upon the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, and whether the standing of those Muslims who stood with him in Mecca was merely an imitation of him, which the Prophet (ﷺ) approved for them. However, 'A'isha held that the obligation of the five daily prayers abrogated the obligation of standing in prayer at night, and she meant that standing in prayer at night had been obligatory upon the Muslims. This is an interpretation (ta'wil). Likewise, there should be no dispute that the first thing God obligated upon the community was the five prayers, which were enjoined on the night of the Ascension (laylat al-mi'raj), and that before them there was no obligation of any prayer upon the community. Had there been, it would have been mentioned in the hadith of the Ascension, which alludes to the five prayers. Also, the obligation of the five prayers upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is like their obligation upon the Muslims. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, for he said: "Standing in prayer at night was abrogated only by the verse ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand in prayer for nearly two-thirds of the night﴾..." And there should be no dispute that the obligation of the five prayers did not abrogate the obligation of standing in prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ), except that it abrogated the requirement of standing for half the night or a little less, and so He abrogated it with ﴿so recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾.

This is shown by the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas on the night he spent in the house of his maternal aunt Maymunah, the mother of the believers, in which he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) slept, and his family with him, until it was midnight, or a little before, or a little after. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) awoke, and he described his ablution, and that he prayed thirteen units (raka'at), then slept again until the caller came to him for the dawn prayer." Ibn 'Abbas was then a boy, so this would have been around the seventh or eighth year after the Hijrah.

It is not reported that the Muslims stood in prayer with him except when he set aside a place in the mosque for his standing in prayer during the nights of Ramadan. His companions heard of this and began slipping away to the mosque to pray with the prayer of their Prophet (ﷺ). Then, on one of the nights, he stayed away from them and said to them: "I feared that it would be made obligatory upon you." This took place in Medina, and 'A'isha was with him, as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah.

[Page 280]

This is clear evidence that the standing in prayer which they performed with the Messenger (ﷺ) was not obligatory upon them, that they did not persist in it, and that none of the night prayer is obligatory upon the Muslims in general. Otherwise, there would be no point in the fear that it would be made obligatory upon them. For if it were assumed that some of the night prayer was obligatory, their standing with the Prophet (ﷺ) would have been the fulfilment of that obligation. This is reinforced by the hadith of Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Hafsah, when she recounted to him a dream that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar had seen: "'Abd Allah is a righteous man; if only he would stand in prayer at night."

The opening of the speech with ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾ implies praise of him for fulfilling the right of the standing in prayer that he was commanded to perform, and that he used to exert himself in it and take it seriously. Then he would limit himself to the prescribed measure, which is half or a little less or more than that. Rather, he took the maximum, which is nearly two-thirds of the night, as is the custom of those of firm resolve (ulu al-'azm). As the Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning His words, ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29], that he fulfilled the longer of the two terms, which was ten years.

It has also come in a hadith that the Prophet (ﷺ) "used to stand in prayer at night until his feet swelled."

The emphasis of the predicate with (inna) indicates its importance. It is a metaphor (kinaya) for his having pleased his Lord by this, and it is a preparation (tawti'a) for the lightening that will be mentioned in His words ﴿so He has turned to you in mercy﴾, so that it is known that it is a lightening of mercy and honour, and so that part of the day is freed for work and jihad.

After the Hijrah, the Prophet's (ﷺ) concerns continued to increase, with the management of the affairs of the Muslims, the defence of Medina, the equipping of armies, and similar matters. Thus, during his days there was no longer the same leisure that he had had during his stay in Mecca. Therefore, the wisdom of God became manifest in lightening for His Messenger (ﷺ) the obligatory part of the night prayer and the voluntary portion (al-raghiba).

In the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, he was asked about the Prophet (ﷺ) when he entered his dwelling, and he said: "When he entered his dwelling, he divided his entrance into three parts: a part for Allah, a part for his family, and a part for himself. Then he divided his part between himself and the people, so he would return that to the special ones (al-khassa) through the general ones (al-'amma), and he would withhold nothing from them. Among them were those with one need, those with two needs, and those with many needs. He would occupy himself with them and occupy them with what would set right their affairs and those of the community, by asking about them and informing them of what was fitting for them."

[Page 281]

The use of the present tense in His words (ya'lamu, "knows") indicates the continuity and renewal of that knowledge, and this is a notification that he is in a state of divine approval.

By contrast, His words ﴿Allah certainly knows those among you who hinder others﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18] are in a context of rebuke, meaning that He has always known that, from time to time, not a portion of it is hidden from Him.

The word (adna) originally means "nearer," from proximity (al-dunuww), and it is used metaphorically for "less." This is because the distance between a thing and what is nearer to it is small. Likewise, "farther" (al-ab'ad) is used metaphorically for "more."

It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyya) for the verb (taqumu, "you stand"), meaning that you stand in a time estimated to be less than two-thirds of the night. That is what exceeds half the night, and it is what His words ﴿or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4] require.

The majority read (thuluthay, "two-thirds") with a damma on the lam, according to the original form. Hisham from Ibn 'Amir read it with a sukun on the lam, for lightness, because some heaviness arose from the dual form.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (﴿nisfahu wa thuluthahu﴾, "its half and its third") with a genitive (khafd) on both, as a conjunction with (﴿thuluthay al-layl﴾, "two-thirds of the night"), meaning: less than its half and less than its third.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (﴿nisfahu wa thuluthahu﴾) with an accusative on both, as objects of (taqumu, "you stand"), meaning: you stand two-thirds of the night, you stand half the night, and you stand a third of the night, in such a way that it does not fall short of the half or of the third. These are different states of the Prophet's (ﷺ) night prayer, following the variation in the nights and days, in their being longer or shorter. All of them fall under the option that God gave him in His words ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except for a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2] up to His words ﴿or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4].

By this, the connection of this clause with the parenthetical clause becomes clear, namely the clause ﴿And Allah determines the night and the day﴾, meaning: Allah has known all of it and informed him of it. Therefore, the meaning does not differ with the differences in the readings. It is strange that al-Farra' said the accusative is closer to correctness.

(Ta'ifa, "a group") is a conjunction with the subject of (inna) in the nominative. This is a permissible construction when it comes after the mention of the predicate of (inna), because its nominative can then be taken as a new independent clause, as in His words ﴿That Allah is free of the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3]. This is one of the subtleties when the attribution of the subject and of the conjoined noun to the predicate differs. Between the standing of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the standing of the group who were with him there is a difference in ruling and in amount. Likewise, Allah's disavowal of the polytheists and His Messenger's disavowal. For the Messenger (ﷺ) calls them, recites the Qur'an to them, and deals with them, whereas Allah is angry with them and curses them. This is the reason for the shift from saying "Indeed, Allah knows that you (plural) stand," to His words ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you (singular) stand﴾, and then His words ﴿and a group﴾, and so on.

The group (ta'ifa) is described as ﴿of those who are with you﴾. If by "being with" is meant true companionship, that is, accompaniment in an act which is the subject of the speech, namely those who accompany you in standing in prayer at night, then the explanation does not identify particular individuals. In the hadith of 'A'isha in Sahih al-Bukhari: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once prayed in the mosque, and some people prayed with his prayer. Then he prayed again the next night, and the people increased. Then they gathered on the third or fourth night, but the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not come out to them. When morning came he said: 'I have seen what you did, and nothing prevented me from coming out to you except that I feared it would be made obligatory upon you.' And that was in Ramadan."

If "being with" is figurative, meaning affiliation, companionship and agreement, then we have counted among them 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, Salman al-Farisi, Abu al-Darda', Zaynab bint Jahsh, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and al-Hawla' bint Tuwayt al-Asadiyya. These were mentioned individually in the hadiths on the night prayer (tahajjud) in Sahih al-Bukhari.

Know that the opening of this verse is an allusion to the praise of the Prophet (ﷺ) for his fulfilling the standing in prayer at night in the fullest manner, and to the praise of the group who followed him in that.

Thus the statement that Allah knows that you stand is meant as a metaphor (kinaya) for His approval of them for what they did.

The purpose is to prepare for His words ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾, to the end of the verse.

For this reason, the verb (ʿalima, "He knows") is repeated in the clause ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are sick﴾, and so on, and it was not said with a conjunction, "and that there will be among you those who are sick."

The clause ﴿and Allah determines the night and the day﴾ is parenthetical (mu'taridha) between the clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾ and the clause ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾. Its connection to the parenthesis has already been explained.

The clause ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ may be a second predicate of (anna), following the predicate in His words ﴿Your Lord knows that you stand for nearly two-thirds of the night﴾, and so on.

It may also be an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for what arises from the clause ﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand﴾, from the listener's expectation to know what that clause prepared for. So, after He thanked them for their action, He lightened the burden for them.

The pronoun in the accusative in (tuhsuhu, "you count it") refers to the standing in prayer which is understood from ﴿that you stand﴾.

Ihsa' (counting) in its real sense is knowing the number of a countable thing. It is derived from the noun (hasa, "pebbles"), the plural of (hasah, "a pebble"), because when they counted a large quantity of something, they put a pebble for each one. Here it is used metaphorically for the ability to bear (al-itaqa). The many acts, such as bowing, prostration and recitation in the night prayer, are likened to countable things. On this basis, al-Hasan and Sufyan explained it. From this is His statement in the hadith: "Be steadfast, but you will not be able to count (lan tuhsu)," meaning: you will not be able to attain complete steadfastness, so take from it according to your capacity.

The (an) here is the light form of the heavy (anna), and its subject is an omitted pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n), whose predicate is the clause. Between (an) and its predicate there is a separation by the negative particle, because the predicate is a verb that is not an invocation nor a non-derivative, according to the customary usage of eloquent Arabic.

The (an) and its clause take the place of the two objects of (ʿalima, "he knew"), since its implied sense is "he knew the non-counting of it by you as a fact."

[p. 284]

It follows from this that Allah says: ﴿So He has turned to you in forgiveness﴾. The verb (tāba, "to turn in forgiveness") is used figuratively for not being held to account before the shortcoming has occurred. Since the shortcoming is anticipated, it resembles the one that has already occurred. So the absence of obligation is expressed by a verb that is used for it, which is the verb (tāba), signifying the lifting of accountability for a sin after it has occurred.

The more likely view is that the address in His words (﴿you cannot keep count of it﴾) and what follows it is directed to the Muslims who used to stand in night prayer. This is either by way of (al-iltifāt, shift) from the third person to the second person after His words ﴿and a group of those with you﴾, or by way of the general term used to mean a specific group (al-'āmm al-murād bihi al-khuṣūṣ), by the indication that the Prophet (ﷺ) would not be presumed unable to keep count, and by the indication of His words ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾, and so on.

The meaning of ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ is: pray what is easy for you. Since prayer does not go without recitation of the Qur'an, this is followed by His words here, ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, meaning: pray, as in His saying, exalted is He, (and the recitation of dawn), meaning the dawn prayer. In using the Qur'an as a metonymy (kināya) for prayer, there is a combination of encouragement to stand in prayer and encouragement to recite the Qur'an in it, by way of conciseness (ījāz).

What is meant is the Qur'an that had been revealed before this Medinan verse, which is a large part of the entire Meccan Qur'an and some of the Medinan. It is not like His words at the beginning of the surah, ﴿and recite the Qur'an in measured tones﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 4], as you have learned there.

His words ﴿what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ mean: what is easy for you of the night prayer. Thus there is no evidence in this verse for the minimum amount of recitation that suffices in prayer, since its context is not this matter. Even if we accept it, "what is easy" is general (mujmal), and it has been clarified by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (al-Fātiḥa)." As for a surah together with the Fātiḥa, it has not been reported from him that he recited in prayer less than one surah, and this is what is obligatory according to the majority of jurists (jumhūr al-fuqahā'). Therefore it is disliked for one praying an obligatory prayer to recite only part of a surah. Reciting the Qur'an in the night, in the night prayers of Ramadan, and in cases of necessity is permissible. In the authentic collection it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) was reciting when he became hoarse, so he bowed, meaning in the middle of the surah.

Abū Ḥanīfa and Aḥmad, in one report from him, said: the recitation of one verse of the Qur'an suffices, even if it is short. The Ḥanafīs give as an example His words (﴿dark green﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 64]). The Opening of the Book is not specified. His two companions differed with him on both points.

The determination of who is obligated to recite, whether a lone worshipper, an imam, or a follower in congregation, is explained in the books of jurisprudence.

When the verb (tāba) is used to mean the acceptance of the repentance of one who repents, it is followed by the preposition (ʿalā) because it implies the meaning of (min). When it means returning from a sin and regretting it, it is followed by whatever preposition fits.

This verse has abrogated the specification of the duration of night prayer as half of it, or a little more, or a little less than a third of it. The specification was accompanied by the amount that is easy, without precise limit. As for the ruling on that night prayer, it remains as explained earlier.

* * *

[p. 285]

﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill, and others traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others fighting in the cause of Allah. So recite of it what is easy, establish prayer, give zakāh, and lend Allah a goodly loan﴾. This sentence is a comprehensive apposition (badal ishtimāl) of the sentence ﴿He knows that you cannot keep count of it﴾. This is another concession, for other circumstances that call for leniency.

This is another wisdom behind abrogating the fixed time for night prayer: taking into account circumstances that befell the Muslims, of the kinds that the condition of the Islamic community calls for. Three kinds are mentioned, which are the basic excuses:

The first kind: excuses of impaired health, which His words ﴿that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ include.

The second kind: the occupations that the necessity of earning a living calls for, such as trade, crafts, farming, and other things. His words ﴿and others traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ point to these. "Allah's bounty" is provision.

The third kind: works for the benefit of the community. His words ﴿and others fighting in the cause of Allah﴾ point to this, and it includes guarding the frontiers and stationing there, managing armies, and what relates to spreading the call of Islam, such as sending delegations and dispatching envoys. All of this is among the affairs of the community in general, and the Prophet (ﷺ) is included in some of them, as in fighting in the cause of Allah and in illness. In the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell ill and did not rise (for night prayer) for a night or two."

If this verse was revealed in Mecca, then it contains good news that the affair of the Muslims will reach independence and a state of superiority over their enemies, so they will fight in the cause of Allah. If it was Medinan, then it is an excuse for them for what they undertook of expeditions and military campaigns.

Some of the Companions used to derive from this verse the virtue of trade and of travel for commerce, since Allah placed those who strive (in fighting) and those who earn lawful wealth on equal footing. That is, Allah mentioned these two causes for abrogating the fixed time of standing in prayer only to honor them, because other excuses are more like illness. The subtleties and nuances of the Qur'an are not limited.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ūd that he said: "Whoever brings something to a city of the cities of the Muslims seeking reward, and sells it at the price of its day, will have the rank of the martyrs with Allah." Then he recited: ﴿and others traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty and others fighting in the cause of Allah﴾.

And from Ibn 'Umar: "Allah has not created a death after death more beloved to me than dying in the cause of Allah, rather than dying between the two saddlebags of my mount, seeking of Allah's bounty while traveling through the land."

If this verse was revealed in Mecca, then it contains good news that the affair of the Muslims is heading toward a state of superiority over their enemy. If it was Medinan, then it is an excuse for them for what befell them.

The meaning of ﴿traveling through the land﴾ is journeying through the land. The literal sense of (ḍarb) is one body striking another. Journeying through the land was called (ḍarb fī al-arḍ, striking through the land) because the verb (yaḍribūn) implicitly carries the meaning of (yasīrūn, they travel). Walking is indeed a striking of the earth by the two feet, but the sense of striking has been forgotten and the meaning of walking is intended. For this reason it takes the preposition (fī), because the earth is the container of the journey, as He said, exalted is He, ﴿So travel through the earth﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 137]. This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿And when you travel through the land, there is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾ [al-Nisā': 101], in the surah of al-Nisā'.

Seeking Allah's bounty means seeking provision. He, exalted is He, said ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 198], meaning trade during the pilgrimage season. So His words ﴿traveling through the land seeking of Allah's bounty﴾ intend by traveling through the land the journey for trade, since travel often occurs at night and also by day, so the traveler needs to sleep during the day.

What follows from this is the same as what followed from the previous clause, so He said ﴿So recite of it what is easy﴾, meaning: of the Qur'an.

The amount of standing in prayer has been tied to what is easy for all Muslims, even though the excuses differ.

This verse required the lifting of the obligation of standing in night prayer from the Muslims, if it had been obligatory on them previously according to one of the two possibilities, or it was an explanation that it had not been made obligatory on them, while they had committed themselves to it. So it clarified to them that what they had committed themselves to, by following the Prophet (ﷺ) in this, is not binding on them.

It gave as the reason for its non-obligation that the community contains many people with excuses that make standing in night prayer burdensome. So Allah did not make it obligatory on them, or He lifted its obligation. Had it not been for consideration of the general presumption (maẓinna ʿāmma), the ruling on standing would have remained in force, and concessions would have been granted to those with excuses only for the duration of their excuse. Thus it becomes clear that this is a legal ruling justified by a presumption (taʿlīl al-ḥukm al-shar'ī bi-al-maẓinna), and the ruling here is negative, that is, the non-imposition. It is like the shortening of prayer during travel, according to the statement of 'Ā'isha, Mother of the Believers: "Prayer was prescribed as two rak'ahs, then it was increased for three of the prayers in the settled state, and the prayer of travel was left as it was." The reason for keeping two rak'ahs is the presumption of hardship during travel.

The concession regarding standing in night prayer is justified by the fact that it was not one of the pillars of Islam, so the religious benefit in it was not strong.

As for the ruling on standing, it is what His words ﴿O you wrapped in garments, stand (in prayer) the night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2] indicate, and what the evidence of exhortation to it from the Sunnah indicates. All of that has already passed.

So this verse is suitable to be a basis for justification by presumption, and it is also suitable to be a basis by which general concessions are analogized, those which take into account the hardship of most of the community, such as the permission of salam sale (a forward sale), rather than individual and particular circumstances.

His words ﴿And establish prayer﴾ are a reminder that the obligatory prayers are those which you must be keen to establish and not neglect, as He said, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at fixed times﴾ [al-Nisā': 103].

In this sequel, by conjoining the command to establish prayer, there is an indication that the five prayers relieve the believers of burden, and that standing in the night is a supererogatory act for them, and in it is much good. Many reports support this, which are in the books of Sunnah.

The conjunction of ﴿and give zakāh﴾ is a completion (tatmīm), because it is generally the case that mention of prayer is not free of being paired with zakāh alongside it. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, derived from this that one who withholds zakāh is to be fought over it. So he said to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "I will surely fight whoever separates prayer from zakāh."

Lending to Allah means voluntary charities, not obligatory ones. Giving charity to the poor is likened to a loan that Allah grants, because Allah promised a great reward for charity, so the state of the giver of charity, responding to Allah's desire for it, resembles that of one who lends to a borrower in that it is fitting that what he lent should return to him. This refers to the reward that will be given on the Day of Recompense.

[p. 288]

Describing the loan as goodly indicates the charity intended for the sake of Allah, the one free from reproach and harm. Goodness varies.

Goodness in each kind is what has the praiseworthy attributes of that kind in its own category. What is praiseworthy in charity is known through the Sharia by what the Qur'an described of the goodness of charities and what came in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning that.

It has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqara His words ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him many times over﴾ [al-Baqara: 245], and in Surat al-Taghābun ﴿If you lend Allah a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you﴾ [al-Taghābun: 17].

* * *

﴿And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward﴾. This is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) for what preceded of the commands in His words ﴿So recite of it what is easy, establish prayer, give zakāh, and lend Allah a goodly loan﴾. His words ﴿any good﴾ include all acts of good.

In the speech there is conciseness by omission (ījāz ḥadhf). The estimated omitted part is: "Do good, and whatever you put forward of it for yourselves, you will find it with Allah." The omitted part is dispensed with by mention of the reward for good.

(Mā) is conditional. The meaning of "putting forward" good is doing it during life. Doing good during the span of life, in hope of benefiting from its reward in the Hereafter, is likened to one who intends to travel sending ahead his baggage, his equipment, and some of his household to the place he intends to reach, so that he will find what benefits him when he arrives.

(Min khayr, of good) is an explanation of the ambiguity of the conditional (mā).

The good (khayr) is what religion describes as beautiful and promises reward for doing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 73, verse 20 (part 3 of 3):

The meaning of (tajiduhu) ("you will find it") is that they will find its recompense and reward, which is what its doer intended. It is as if they find the very thing they sent forward. This usage is very common in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, where the recompense or return for a thing is expressed by the name of the thing it is exchanged for and repaid with. From this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying about the one who hoards wealth and does not pay its due: "It will be represented to him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald, venomous snake, which will seize him by his two cheeks and say: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'"

The pronoun referring to the absent (the "-hu" in tajiduhu) is the first object of (tajiduu) ("you find"), and its second object is (khayran) ("better").

[Page 289]

The detached pronoun between them is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and its occurring between a definite and an indefinite noun is permissible, contrary to the common view about the nature of the pronoun of separation, which requires it to occur between two definites. This is because (afʿala min kadhā) ("more ... than such-and-such", the elative form) resembles the definite in that the definite article cannot be attached to it.

(Khayran) is an elative (ism al-tafḍīl), meaning "better than what you send forward." The intended sense is not that you will find it to be of the same kind as good, but that the reward is multiplied, in accordance with what is indicated by His saying: ﴿If you lend to God a goodly loan, He will multiply it for you﴾ [al-Taghabun: 17], and by many other verses.

The pronoun of separation here serves merely to emphasise and confirm the statement.

The coordination of ﴿and greater in reward﴾ with (khayran) is either as a coordinated element, or the emphasis of the pronoun of separation extends to it.

(Ajran) ("in reward") is in the accusative as a specifying accusative (tamyīz al-nisba) after (aʿẓama) ("greater"), because it carries the sense of a verb. The underlying construction is: "and greater is its reward," just as you say: "I found him outstretched in the palm," and the meaning is that its reward is better and greater than what you sent forward.
