﴿And seek forgiveness from God; surely God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾. The conjunction (wāw) may be coordinating, so that this clause is coordinated with the clause ﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾ and so on. It then has the status of a concluding statement (tadhyīl), giving guidance to make up for any shortcoming in some of the good that God has commanded them to send forward. This includes the obligatory duties, where a shortcoming in some of them calls for repentance.

The conjunction may also be resumptive (lil-istiʾnāf), and the clause is then an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī) arising from the permission to omit part of the night prayer. It is God's guidance toward what fills the place of the night prayer, whose omission is a risk, by the Muslim asking forgiveness from his Lord when he wakes during parts of the night. This is included in His saying: ﴿And at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 18]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when the last third of the night remains, and says: 'Whoever calls upon Me, I will answer him; whoever asks of Me, I will give him; whoever seeks forgiveness from Me, I will forgive him.'" He also said: "Whoever wakes in the night and says: 'There is no god but God alone, He has no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs praise, and He is over all things capable. Praise belongs to God, glory be to God, there is no god but God, God is greatest, and there is no power nor strength except by God,' then says: 'O God, forgive me,' or makes a supplication, it will be answered for him."

The clause ﴿surely God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for the command to seek forgiveness, that is: because God is abundant in forgiveness and intensely merciful. The purpose of this justification is to encourage and urge seeking forgiveness, since it is hoped to be answered. The use of the two attributes, which indicate intensity in the quality, implies a promise that it will be answered.

Surat al-Muddaththir

It is called in the books of tafsir (exegesis) "Surat al-Muddaththir," and it is so named in the mushafs (copies of the Qur'an) that we have seen, among them manuscripts in Qayrawan from the fifth century.

By al-Muddaththir is meant the Prophet ﷺ, described by the state in which he was addressed, just as some surahs were named after the prophets mentioned in them.

Alternatively, it is named by the word that occurs in it, similar to what was mentioned earlier concerning the naming of "Surat al-Muzzammil," and like what preceded in surah al-Mujadila regarding the possibility of pronouncing the dal with a fatha or a kasra.

It is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi reported the consensus on this. Al-Suyuti did not mention it in al-Itqan among the surahs some of which are Medinan. Al-Alusi mentioned that the author of al-Tahrir, Muhammad ibn al-Naqib al-Maqdisi, who died in the year 698 AH, has a tafsir, and that he mentioned the statement of Muqatil, or his statement, concerning ﴿And We have made their number only a trial﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31], "it was revealed at Medina." I have not found the chain for this, nor have I seen this attributed to anyone else, and it will come.

[Page 292]

It has been said that it is the second surah in order of revelation, and that nothing was revealed before it except the surah (﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1]). This is what came in the hadith of ʿĀʾisha in the two Sahihs, concerning the description of the beginning of revelation: the Truth came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was in the cave of Hira, the angel came to him and said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1] up to ﴿what he did not know﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 5]. Then she said: "Then the revelation paused." She did not mention the revelation of any verses after the verses of ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾.

Likewise is the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, transmitted through Abu Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, through many chains with wordings that vary among them. The sum of what is gathered from its chains: Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, speaking about the pause in revelation, said in his narration that the Prophet ﷺ said: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky, and I was called. I looked before me, behind me, to my right, and to my left, and I saw nothing. Then I raised my head, and behold, the angel who had come to me at Hira was sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth. I was overcome with terror from him, so I came to Khadija and said: 'Cover me, cover me,' and they covered me." Other than Ibn Shihab added in his narration: "And pour cold water over me, and they covered me and poured cold water over me." Al-Nawawi said: pouring water is to calm fear. Then God revealed: ﴿O you wrapped up﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1] up to ﴿and abomination, shun﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 5]. Then revelation became vigorous and continuous.

It occurs in Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, that it is the first of the Qur'an, Surat al-Muddaththir. The one who narrates in his hadith that the Messenger of God spoke about the pause in revelation is the same one, and a pause occurs between two things, so it requires that a revelation came before Surat al-Muddaththir, which is what was clarified in the hadith of ʿĀʾisha.

Earlier, at the beginning of Surat al-Muzzammil, Jabir ibn Zayd's statement was mentioned: that Surat al-Qalam was revealed after Surat al-ʿAlaq, that Surat al-Muzzammil is third, and that Surat al-Muddaththir is fourth.

Jabir ibn Zayd also said: after al-Muddaththir, Surat al-Fatiha was revealed. There is no doubt that Surat al-Muddaththir was revealed before al-Muzzammil, and that the opposition of the polytheists had increased after the revelation of Surat al-Muddaththir, so the address to them in Surat al-Muzzammil was more extensive.

It occurs in the hadith of Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah in Sahih al-Bukhari and Jami al-Tirmidhi, through the chain of Ibn Shihab, that the revelation of this surah was before the prayer was prescribed.

The prayer was prescribed after the pause in revelation, whether the number was five or fewer, and whether it was obligatory, as is the apparent meaning of their saying "it was prescribed," or whether "prescribed" means "legislated." The duration of the pause in revelation

[Page 293]

is greatly disputed. It has been said it lasted two and a half years, it has been said forty days, and it has been said fifteen days. The soundest view is that it lasted forty days. It appears, therefore, that al-Muddaththir was revealed in the first year of the mission, and that the prayer was prescribed immediately after, as the arrangement of Ibn Ishaq in setting out the events of his biography suggests.

The people of Medina, in their final count which they adopted, and the people of Syria, counted its verses as fifty-five. The people of Basra and Kufa, and the people of Medina in their first count, which they later abandoned, counted it as fifty-six.

Its purposes

Among its purposes: the honouring of the Prophet ﷺ, and the command to convey the call of the message.

The proclamation of God's oneness in divinity.

The command to purify oneself physically and spiritually.

The rejection of idols.

Giving abundant charity.

The command to be patient.

The warning to the polytheists of the terror of resurrection.

The threat against one who undertakes to attack the Qur'an, claiming it to be human speech, and the disbelief of the attacker in God's blessing upon him, for he proceeds to attack His verses while knowing they are true.

The description of the horrors of Hell.

The refutation of the polytheists who made light of it and claimed that its guardians were few.

The challenge to the People of the Book, that they were ignorant of the number of its guardians.

The despairing of them from escaping punishment.

The depiction of their misguidance in this world.

And the contrast between their state and the state of the believers, the people of prayer, almsgiving, and belief in the Day of Recompense.
